report:
## Research Summary

The scientific consensus, based on the highest-quality evidence, does **not** support the claim that increasing the number of childhood vaccines causes autism.

**Key evidence against the claim:**
- A large CDC-affiliated study (DeStefano et al., 2013) examined over 1,000 children and specifically tested whether the *number* of vaccine antigens received in early childhood was associated with autism risk. It found **no association** between antigen exposure/vaccine number and autism (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/pds.3482; https://www.jpeds.com/article/S0022-3476(13)00666-5/fulltext). Notably, even though the *number of vaccines* on the schedule has increased, the total *antigen* load has actually decreased due to improved vaccine formulations.
- A 2025 Danish study of 1.2 million children found no link between vaccine components (including aluminum adjuvants) and autism or 49 other chronic conditions (https://en.ssi.dk/news/news/2025/large-danish-study-no-link-between-vaccines-and-autism-or-49-other-health-conditions).
- A comprehensive review (PMC, 2022) states that the "great majority of scientists, physicians, and public health researchers" have refuted causation between vaccines and autism after extensive study (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8694782/).

**On the pro-claim studies:** Some smaller studies claiming vaccinated children have higher autism/neurodevelopmental disorder rates (e.g., Mawson et al.) rely on parent-reported surveys of "convenience samples" (like homeschooling groups) rather than randomized or robustly controlled designs, introducing significant selection and recall bias. One such Mawson paper was retracted after heavy methodological criticism (https://retractionwatch.com/2016/11/28/study-linking-vaccines-autism-pulled-frontiers-following-heavy-criticism/).

**Note:** CDC's own website recently added contested language suggesting the causal question isn't fully settled, but independent fact-checkers and most scientists dispute this framing, calling it not evidence-based.

**Conclusion:** The weight of rigorous, peer-reviewed evidence contradicts the claim; assertions to the contrary largely stem from methodologically weak or retracted studies.
